text: Host/authority confusion in parse-url's git-ssh fallback: attacker-controlled `url` reaches `parsed.href.match(GIT_RE)` (src/index.js:67), and `parsed.resource` and `parsed.host` are then assigned from `matched[4]` (src/index.js:71-72) — capture group 4 of GIT_RE is `([\w\.\-@]+)`, a greedy class that PERMITS the `@` character. For an input that parse-path marks `parse_failed` (e.g. `https://evil.com@good.com/p` or `git@evil.com@good.com/x`), group 4 greedily captures the entire `evil.com@good.com` span, so the returned `host`/`resource` is not the true URL authority. Consumers of parse-url use `parsed.resource`/`parsed.host` to choose a connection target or to make allowlist/host-validation decisions, so the returned authority disagrees with what an HTTP/SSH client would actually contact — SSRF / access-control bypass. Note the hand-rolled regex OVERRIDES the real parser's output rather than validating it, and `parsed.parse_failed` is reset to false (L75) so callers see the result as a clean parse.

The missing control is a try/catch around the external parser calls that normalizes failures into the library's own error type.

text: In src/index.js:66-75, the git-ssh fallback REVERTS the parse-failure safety flag it just branched on. Line 66 does `if (parsed.parse_failed) {`, and after synthesizing fields from the permissive GIT_RE regex, line 75 does `parsed.parse_failed = false`. So when parse-path's real parser FAILS on an attacker-supplied url, parse-url overwrites the failure indicator back to `false` and hands the caller an object that advertises a successful parse, with `protocol`/`protocols`/`host`/`resource`/`user`/`pathname` fabricated from regex capture groups rather than from an actual URL parse. Any consumer that uses `parse_failed` as its validation gate (it is a documented public output field — JSDoc src/index.js:33 lists '`parse_failed` (Boolean): Whether the parsing failed or not.') is told the url is good precisely in the case where parsing broke. This is a protection disabled in-code, sitting directly on the live attacker-reachable path.

The normalization sanitizer is OFF BY DEFAULT, and the shipped example documents normalization as 'automatic' — a doc/code mismatch consistent with the default having been reverted from on to off. src/index.js:35 declares `const parseUrl = (url, normalize = false)`, lowered in the CPG to `normalize = normalize === void 0 ? false : normalize`, so the normalizeUrl() call at line 60 is skipped entirely unless a caller explicitly opts in. Meanwhile example/index.js:34 carries the comment 'If you want to parse fancy Git urls, turn off the automatic url normalization' immediately above `parseUrl("git+ssh://git@host.xz/path/name.git", false)` — i.e. the example tells users to 'turn off' a normalization it calls 'automatic', and passes an explicit `false` that is already the default and therefore redundant. That redundant explicit `false` plus the stale 'automatic' wording are the tell that this default was previously true (protection on) and was flipped to false. Net effect today: raw attacker-controlled `url` reaches parsePath() at line 63 unnormalized on the default path.

The only DoS/length protection in parse-url is a PUBLICLY MUTABLE static whose own error message instructs callers to raise it. src/index.js:50 guards with `url.length > parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH`, and src/index.js:84 sets `parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = 2048` as an ordinary writable property on the exported function (exported at line 86 via `exports["default"] = parseUrl`). The throwErr message at line 51 reads verbatim: 'Input exceeds maximum length. If needed, change the value of parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH.' — the library itself documents its sole input-size protection as something to turn up/off. Because the check reads the property at call time (line 50 is reachable_from_entry=true) while the initializer at line 84 is module-level (reachable_from_entry=false), any consumer or any other code sharing the process can do `parseUrl.MAX_INPUT_LENGTH = Infinity` and re-enable unbounded attacker input into the GIT_RE backtracking regex at line 38 and into parsePath() at line 63. The existence of this cap is itself evidence the maintainer knew long inputs were dangerous here.

The JSDoc contains an explicit acknowledgement that the normalization protection does not cover the ssh/git path — 'For SSH urls, normalize won't work.' (src/index.js:19, inside the parseUrl doc block). That documented gap lines up exactly with the GIT_RE fallback at lines 66-75, which is the branch that fabricates security-relevant output fields. Concretely, GIT_RE at line 38 accepts `http(s)?:\/\/` in its first alternative, and its capture group 4 is `([\w\.\-@]+)` which PERMITS the `@` character; that group is assigned to BOTH `parsed.resource` (line 71) and `parsed.host` (line 72) while `parsed.protocol` is hard-overwritten to the string 'ssh' (line 70) and `parsed.protocols` to ['ssh'] (line 69). So an http(s)-prefixed input that fails parse-path gets relabelled with protocol 'ssh' and a `host` that may embed userinfo — protocol and host confusion in the returned object, which is the SSRF-relevant decision data consumers act on. The maintainer-documented 'normalize won't work' note means the one sanitizer in the file is known not to defend this path.

The GIT_RE literal at src/index.js:38 captures the "host" with the character class ([\w\.\-@]+), which includes the userinfo delimiter '@'. Capture group 4 is then assigned verbatim to BOTH parsed.resource (line 71) and parsed.host (line 72). Because '@' is an allowed host character, a URL such as "git@github.com@evil.com:path" has group 4 greedily capture "github.com@evil.com", so parsed.host is not a hostname at all but a userinfo+host pair. Under SSH/URL semantics the effective host is the LAST @-segment (evil.com), so a downstream consumer that allowlists on parsed.host with a prefix/startsWith/contains check on "github.com" passes the check while the connection actually targets evil.com -- host-spoofing leading to SSRF. The danger is entirely in the literal's character class, not in the match() call. PRECONDITION the verifier must confirm: this branch only executes when parsed.parse_failed is true (line 66), i.e. only for inputs that parse-path itself failed to parse, so the verifier should check whether parse-path fails on a double-'@' git URL.
